name: Fall Risk Monitoring
title: Fall Risk Monitoring
answer: Fall risk monitoring covers the prediction and prevention of unplanned falls among hospital inpatients, with particular attention to intensive care and step down units where sedation, delirium, weakness, and attached lines raise risk. It includes risk scores generated from nursing assessments, medication lists, vital signs, mobility notes, and sensor data, plus the alerts and care processes that follow. The scope also takes in the monitoring of patients after discharge from critical care, where deconditioning and new medications can change fall risk. It is a predictive patient analytics application rather than a general wellness or community fall prevention program.

sections.body: Fall risk monitoring covers the prediction and prevention of unplanned falls among hospital inpatients, with particular attention to intensive care and step down units where sedation, delirium, weakness, and attached lines raise risk. It includes risk scores generated from nursing assessments, medication lists, vital signs, mobility notes, and sensor data, plus the alerts and care processes that follow. The scope also takes in the monitoring of patients after discharge from critical care, where deconditioning and new medications can change fall risk. It is a predictive patient analytics application rather than a general wellness or community fall prevention program.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Fall risk monitoring runs on the hospital's electronic health record and related clinical data systems, pulling nursing flowsheets, medication administration records, laboratory results, and vital signs into a common view. Bed and chair sensors, wearable accelerometers, real time location systems, and in some units depth cameras or video analytics feed additional signals. The models themselves typically run on hospital servers or a cloud environment, with results surfaced in the electronic health record, a nursing dashboard, or a mobile device. Integration with nurse call systems and alarm management platforms determines whether an alert reaches the right person at the right time.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with defining the outcome, usually an inpatient fall documented in the record, and assembling a retrospective dataset with features such as age, mobility status, cognitive state, medications, and recent vital signs. Because falls are relatively uncommon, teams often use class weighting, resampling, or careful threshold selection to balance sensitivity and false alerts. Common model choices include logistic regression, gradient boosted trees, and neural networks, though the choice matters less than validation on the local patient population. Nurses then receive a risk score or alert, combine it with bedside judgment, and document any prevention steps such as toileting schedules, bed alarms, or mobility assistance. Performance is monitored over time for drift, alert fatigue, and changes in documentation practice.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Fall risk monitoring handles protected health information, so privacy, access control, deidentification for secondary use, and audit trails are central concerns. Models can encode bias if training data underrepresent older adults, patients with cognitive impairment, or specific racial and ethnic groups, and a false negative may delay prevention while a false positive adds to alarm fatigue. Provenance matters: teams need to know which data trained the model, which version is deployed, how it was validated, and who reviewed changes. The site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which reflects the broader litigation exposure that hospitals and vendors consider when adopting predictive tools. Regulatory pathways for software as a medical device, clinical validation, and local governance review all shape what can be deployed and how it is monitored.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward continuous, multimodal monitoring that combines electronic health record data with wearable sensors, ambient sensing, and computer vision to detect changes in gait, mobility, and confusion earlier. Predictive models are likely to become more personalized, using a patient's own baseline rather than a single population threshold, and more integrated with early warning systems for deterioration. Privacy preserving methods such as federated learning and on device inference may reduce the need to move raw patient data. The main open questions are whether these systems improve outcomes in rigorous trials, how they fit nursing workflows without adding alert burden, and how responsibility is shared when a prediction is wrong.
